Gazingstock
gā'zing-stok
n. (a person set up to be stared at; an object of public spectacle and contempt)
A compound of gazing and stock in the old sense of a stump or post — a thing set up for people to look at. It renders Greek theatrizo, to make a theatre-show of, and a Hebrew term for public disgrace in Nahum.

Biblical Definition

Nahum uses the word for the sentence on Nineveh: “And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock” (Nahum 3:6). Public shaming is there a judgment of God on a cruel city. The writer to the Hebrews then applies the same idea to the church, and reverses its meaning: “Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used” (Hebrews 10:33). He is calling them to remember the former days “in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions” (Hebrews 10:32) — and the memory is offered as an encouragement, not an embarrassment. Paul uses the same figure of the apostles: “we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men” (1 Corinthians 4:9). The believer is therefore warned that a measure of public contempt belongs to the calling, and the two halves of Hebrews 10:33 divide the whole church between them — some are the spectacle, and the rest are those who stood publicly with them, which in a season of reproach is the costlier half.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a gazing-stock as a person gazed at with scorn or abhorrence, an object of curiosity or contempt.

expand to see more

GAZING-STOCK, n. A person gazed at with scorn or abhorrence; an object of curiosity or contempt.

GAZE, v.i. To fix the eyes and look steadily and earnestly; to look with eagerness or curiosity, as in admiration, astonishment, or with study.

SPECTACLE, n. A show; a gazing stock; something exhibited to view.

REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; contumelious or opprobrious language.

COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 10:33 — "Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used."

Hebrews 10:32 — "But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions;"

1 Corinthians 4:9 — "For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men."

Nahum 3:6 — "And I will cast abominable filth upon thee, and make thee vile, and will set thee as a gazingstock."

Modern Corruption

Public shaming is now an instrument the church is tempted to wield rather than a reproach it is called to bear.

expand to see more

The gazingstock is a technology, and our age has industrialised it. What once required a magistrate and a marketplace now takes a phone, and the crowd is unlimited. Believers are on both ends of it. Where the church is despised, Hebrews 10 is exactly the passage for the moment; the reproach is expected, and the memory of having endured it is a comfort rather than a grievance. But where believers themselves have taken up the instrument — circulating an accusation, joining a pile-on, making a spectacle of an offender for an audience — they have adopted a method Scripture assigns to the judgment of Nineveh and to the enemies of the apostles. The rule of Matthew 18 is a private word first, and the crowd last, and it was written against precisely this appetite.

The second half of Hebrews 10:33 is the harder application and the one usually skipped. The congregation is commended not only for being made a spectacle but for becoming companions of them that were so used — standing publicly beside people already under reproach, and taking the reproach onto themselves. That is a costlier obedience than enduring one's own shame, because it is voluntary. It is also the plain duty of a church when one of its members, or a faithful minister elsewhere, is being made a gazingstock for the truth's sake.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek theatrizo (G2301), to make a public show of — Hebrews 10:33, its only occurrence; theatron (G2302), a spectacle — 1 Corinthians 4:9.

expand to see more

Greek theatrizo (G2301) — to expose as in a theatre; Hebrews 10:33, its only occurrence in the New Testament.

Greek theatron (G2302) — a theatre, hence a spectacle; 1 Corinthians 4:9, and the literal building at Acts 19:29.

Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach; Hebrews 10:33, and Hebrews 11:26 of the reproach of Christ that Moses esteemed greater riches.

Greek koinonos (G2844) — a partner, companion; Hebrews 10:33, of those who stood with the reproached.

Nahum 3:6 shows the same treatment as a divine judgment on a cruel city — the shame is deserved there, and undeserved in Hebrews.

Usage

"“Ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions” — remembered as honour, not humiliation."

"“Companions of them that were so used” — standing beside the reproached is the costlier half."

"“A spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men” — the apostolic estimate of the ministry."
